name: Moxi laser

lead: Moxi is a light fractional laser on the Sciton platform that works at 1927 nm. People use it for brown spots, sun damage and skin texture, seeking brighter, more even skin with lighter downtime than ablative resurfacing.

It treats a pattern of microscopic zones of skin, which are replaced during healing, leaving skin between them intact. A 2023 study examined a fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes, and two completed registered studies tested the wavelength for diffuse pigmentation (30 participants) and hyperpigmentation in Fitzpatrick skin types V and VI (15 participants).

paras: It is a clinic procedure, usually done in a series of sessions. Skin typically looks pink and feels rough for a few days as treated zones shed. People often schedule it around sun avoidance.
Registry entries do not summarise adverse effects. Pigment changes are a general concern with lasers, particularly in darker skin. It is a clinic-only procedure.

angle.text: Moxi's 1927-nm fractional laser clears surface pigment and renews texture with lighter downtime, leaving brighter, more even skin. It is used for pigmentation and sun damage, and registered studies of 15 to 30 participants exist.

lead: Moxi is a light fractional laser treatment from Sciton that uses a 1927-nm wavelength, as indicated by registered studies describing a fractionated 1927-nm laser and a trial combining BBL, Moxi (fractionated 1927) and Halo. It is used in clinics for pigmentation, sun damage and skin texture.

Published evidence is small. A 2023 study examined a fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes[1], and two completed registered studies tested the wavelength for diffuse pigmentation (30 participants) and for hyperpigmentation in Fitzpatrick skin types V and VI (15 participants).[2][3] Fractional lasers treat columns of skin and leave surrounding tissue intact, and are described as lighter than ablative resurfacing.

paras: Registered studies list skin pigment, diffuse pigmentation, actinic changes and hyperpigmentation.[1][2][3] In practice it is often combined with BBL and Halo in a single session, as in a 15-person pilot.

NCT05226104 is a completed 30-participant study of fractionated 1927 nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes, and NCT05493280 is a completed 15-participant study in darker skin types.[2][3] A published 2023 study reports on diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes.[1] The studies are small, and registry entries here do not summarise outcomes or adverse events.
